planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun on well-drained soil, pairing this female Latvian selection with a male pollinator such as 'Lord' within about 50 feet for reliable fruit set.

directions: Sunny is a Latvian-origin female sea buckthorn selection bred for unusually large, mild, less-acidic berries and notably fewer thorns than older Russian types, making harvest by hand somewhat easier. Give it lean, well-drained soil in full sun; the nitrogen-fixing roots actually perform poorly in rich garden loam and prefer sandy or gravelly sites. As a dioecious shrub it produces no fruit without a nearby male vine in bloom at the same time, so plan for a pollinator from the start. Because Latvian-bred stock tends to tolerate erratic winter freeze-thaw cycles better than some German cultivars, it is a solid choice for continental climates with unpredictable late-winter warm spells.
sources: Hardy Fruit Tree Nursery — Sea Buckthorn Cultivar Notes
University of Saskatchewan Fruit Program
USDA Agricultural Research Service

planting.note: Plant this vigorous German female cultivar in spring in full sun on lean, well-drained soil, with a male pollinator such as 'Pollmix' planted within about 50-100 feet.

directions: Askola was selected in former East Germany and is prized among small-scale growers for exceptionally high vitamin C and E content in its late-August-ripening orange fruit, along with some of the strongest, most vigorous shoot growth of any commonly grown sea buckthorn cultivar. That vigor means it benefits from an annual thinning cut to remove crowded interior wood and keep the thorny canopy manageable for hand or branch harvest. Like all sea buckthorn, its nitrogen-fixing root system tolerates poor, sandy, or coastal soils that would stunt most other fruiting shrubs, but it dislikes waterlogged ground. Being dioecious, it requires a male plant nearby to set any fruit at all.
sources: Raintree Nursery — Askola Seaberry
Jeffries Nurseries — Sea Buckthorn Cultivars
Julius Kühn Institute — German Sea Buckthorn Breeding Program

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun on lean, well-drained soil; Habego is a female cultivar and needs a male sea buckthorn nearby for pollination.

directions: Habego is a German-bred female sea buckthorn certified for commercial propagation alongside the cultivar 'Sirola' in the mid-2000s, and it shares the strong, upright shoot growth typical of the modern German breeding line, though it generally yields somewhat less fruit per bush than older selections like 'Hergo' or 'Askola'. Its orange berries ripen in late summer in tight clusters along second-year wood and are best harvested by cutting whole fruiting branches, since the tart fruit clings tightly and bruises if picked by hand. Grow it in poor, sandy, or rocky soil in full sun, where its nitrogen-fixing roots give it a real advantage over less tolerant fruiting shrubs, and avoid heavy, poorly drained clay. Prune only to remove crossing or dead wood, since flower buds form on the previous season's growth.
sources: Agroforestry Research Trust — Sea Buckthorn Cultivars
Julius Kühn Institute — German Sea Buckthorn Breeding Program
USDA Agricultural Research Service

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in early spring in full sun to part shade; Hugin is self-fertile and sets a full crop without a second aronia nearby.

directions: Hugin is a Scandinavian-bred black chokeberry selected for a noticeably more compact, tidy habit than seed-grown Aronia melanocarpa, named for one of the two ravens of Norse mythology and well suited to smaller gardens where full-size aronia would sprawl. It flowers profusely in spring with white clusters that draw pollinators, then sets heavy loads of shiny black, tannin-rich berries best used for juice, syrup, or jam rather than fresh eating, since raw fruit is quite astringent. Fall color is a strong point, turning brilliant orange-red well before most other fruiting shrubs color up. It tolerates wet or boggy soil far better than most berry shrubs but performs poorly on shallow, chalky ground, so amend heavy alkaline soils before planting.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Aronia melanocarpa 'Hugin'
Panglobal Plants — Aronia Cultivar Notes
University of Minnesota Extension — Aronia Cultivar Selection

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring alongside a compatible early-blooming pollinizer, since Vostorg, like most haskap, is self-infertile.

directions: Vostorg is a Siberian-bred haskap released in the early 2010s and known for consistently large, heavily wax-coated blue-violet fruit — often over an inch long — and for carrying some of the highest vitamin C content measured among haskap cultivars in comparative trials. The sweet-tart flavor with a pronounced sour edge makes it popular fresh as well as processed. Like other haskap, it flowers very early in spring, often weeks before other fruiting shrubs, so choose a planting site that avoids frost pockets even though open blooms tolerate light freezes. Vostorg's Siberian origin gives it outstanding cold hardiness but, as with other haskap, it struggles in hot, humid summer climates and is best reserved for short-season northern gardens.
sources: Zahradnictvo Limbach — Vostorg Honeyberry Cultivar Notes
Oregon State University Extension — Haskap/Honeyberry Production
Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada — Honeyberry Cultivar Trials

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring in full sun; despite marketing as a stand-alone selection, fruit set and size improve noticeably with a second haskap cultivar planted nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Sold under the Proven Winners Yezberry trademark, 'Kapu' descends from purely Japanese Lonicera caerulea strains rather than the Russian and Kuril lines behind most other haskap breeding, giving it a more compact, rounded form and large, tangy fruit borne over a longer harvest window than many single-flush cultivars. It tolerates winter cold to roughly -30F and needs very little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood in its first several years. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; while it is marketed as capable of some self-fruiting, yields are markedly higher with a genetically distinct haskap cultivar blooming nearby at the same time. As with all haskap, it flowers extremely early in spring and performs best in cool-summer regions rather than the humid South.
sources: Proven Winners — Yezberry Solo Japanese Haskap
US Plant Patent PP26,820 — Lonicera caerulea 'Kapu'
Oregon State University Extension — Haskap/Honeyberry Production

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very acidic, moist, well-drained soil; Ida is self-fertile and, like other lingonberry cultivars, can produce a smaller summer crop followed by a larger fall crop.

directions: Ida was developed at Sweden's Balsgård research station and stood out in USDA-ARS comparative trials for having notably higher anthocyanin content than several sibling Swedish cultivars, giving its berries a deeper red color. It forms the same low, glossy-leaved evergreen mat typical of the species, spreading gradually by rhizomes into a dense groundcover over a few seasons. Grow it in very acidic, humus-rich soil in the pH 4.5-5.5 range, ideally in the light shade of taller acid-loving shrubs like blueberry or rhododendron. Renew older plantings by shearing back hard every few years to stimulate fresh, more productive growth.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Lingonberry Cultivar Trials, Corvallis OR
NordGen — Lingonberry Plant Portrait
Oregon State University Extension — Lingonberry Cultivar Evaluation

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very acidic, moist, well-drained soil; Linnea is self-fertile and forms a dense low mat over its first few seasons.

directions: Linnea was selected in Sweden from an open-pollinated seedling of the older wild-derived cultivar 'Sanna' and is grown as a somewhat newer, more refined alternative within the same Scandinavian lingonberry breeding line. Like its parent, it produces glossy evergreen foliage year-round and small pink-tinged bell flowers in late spring, followed by tart red berries in two flushes per season. It requires the same very acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil as blueberry and performs best with light shade rather than baking full sun in warmer parts of its hardiness range. Because lingonberry spreads slowly by underground rhizomes, space plants closely if a solid groundcover is the goal, or wider if used as an edging plant.
sources: Fedco Seeds — Linnea Lingonberry
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Lingonberry Cultivar Trials, Corvallis OR
NordGen — Lingonberry Plant Portrait

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very acidic, moist, well-drained soil; Sanna is one of the older Swedish selections and serves as breeding stock for several newer cultivars.

directions: Sanna is a foundational Swedish lingonberry selection made directly from a superior wild strain rather than through controlled crossing, and it later served as the seed parent behind the newer cultivar 'Linnea'. It grows as a compact, spreading evergreen groundcover with the species' typical small, leathery, boxwood-like leaves and clusters of tart red berries produced in two harvests a season. Provide the same acidic, moisture-retentive conditions favored by blueberries and cranberries, ideally with a mulch of pine needles or acidic compost to maintain soil pH. Light afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch in hotter parts of its hardiness range, while full sun in cooler climates produces the heaviest fruit set.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Lingonberry Cultivar Trials, Corvallis OR
NordGen — Lingonberry Plant Portrait
Oregon State University Extension — Lingonberry Cultivar Evaluation

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very acidic, moist, well-drained soil; Splendor was bred at Sweden's now-closed Balsgård research station alongside several other named lingonberry cultivars.

directions: Splendor emerged from the Balsgård fruit breeding program in southern Sweden, the same research station responsible for several other named lingonberry selections evaluated side by side in North American trials. It shares the species' dense, low, evergreen habit and produces small white to pale pink spring flowers followed by glossy red berries prized for their sharp, cranberry-like tartness in Scandinavian preserves. Because lingonberry roots are shallow and fine, keep the planting bed consistently moist but never waterlogged, and avoid cultivating around the base to prevent rhizome damage. A topdressing of acidic mulch each spring helps maintain the low soil pH the plant needs to take up nutrients effectively.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Lingonberry Cultivar Trials, Corvallis OR
NordGen — Lingonberry Plant Portrait
Oregon State University Extension — Lingonberry Cultivar Evaluation
